idiom_name: requestAnimationFrame(time => ...) frame callback with a lag accumulator
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types over the same browser contract: requestAnimationFrame takes a FrameRequestCallback whose argument is a DOMHighResTimeStamp 'indicating the end of the previous frame's rendering', and the callback 'must call requestAnimationFrame() again' because the request is one-shot. What replaces the classic structure: nothing at runtime - the accumulator and clamp are plain code; the types make units and handles explicit, so a NodeJS.Timeout or a millisecond value cannot silently stand in for a frame handle or a seconds delta. Keep the frame callback typed and thin (FrameRequestCallback), let the simulation step be a pure typed function of dt, and remember the DOM lib must be part of the tsconfig for these types to exist.
pitfalls: Type erasure leaves unit errors unchecked: DOMHighResTimeStamp is a millisecond number with no brand distinguishing it from seconds or a frame count - name every conversion once.
The DOM lib's rAF types exist only when tsconfig includes the DOM library; a Node target compiles similar code yet has no requestAnimationFrame, so target-specific loops must be split.
TypeScript's type system cannot see the loop's runtime hazards (one-shot re-arm, tab pause, clamped lag); the accumulator still needs review and tests.
cancelAnimationFrame expects the handle rAF returned; typing it as anything but number invites cross-target mistakes between browser and Node typings.

variants.name: Node.js manual loop with timers and a monotonic clock (typed)
variants.implementation_notes: For Node targets TypeScript has the same manual shape as JavaScript with different types: timers 'implement a similar API as the timers API provided by Web Browsers but use a different internal implementation that is built around the Node.js Event Loop', setTimeout returns a NodeJS.Timeout, and performance.now() supplies a monotonic millisecond timestamp for the accumulator. What replaces the classic structure: hand-write the driver - a recursive setTimeout (or setImmediate) re-arms the loop and the delay is only a pacing hint, since timers fire late and never early. Use it for headless simulations, tick servers and tools; clamp accumulated lag so a busy event loop cannot spiral, and keep the frame state typed in a small loop struct.
pitfalls: setTimeout on a busy event loop fires late; measure elapsed time with performance.now() and never use the requested delay as dt.
Timers are not a fixed-step source: callback cadence drifts with the event loop's phases, so counting callbacks diverges from real time.
A thrown exception breaks the recursion and stops the loop; wrap the body or re-arm before work.
Node's performance.now() comes from node:perf_hooks and must not be confused with Date.now(), which is wall-clock time.
